notes.meaning: Peter greets his readers as a servant and apostle, meaning a messenger sent with the authority of Jesus Christ. He writes to believers who have received the very same precious faith shared by the apostles. This gift comes not through human effort, but through the righteousness of Jesus Christ, whom Peter calls our God and Savior.

Peter prays that God's grace, which is His unearned favor, and deep inner peace will richly increase in the lives of his readers. These blessings are not gained by mere human intellect. They grow as believers come to know God and Jesus our Lord through a living, personal relationship.

God's own divine power has already provided believers with everything needed for spiritual life and holy living. We receive these resources by knowing Christ, who called us to Himself by His own glorious excellence. Believers do not need extra secret teachings, because Christ has already equipped them completely.

Through His glorious power, Christ has given believers magnificent and valuable promises. By trusting these promises, Christians escape the moral rot of sinful worldly desires and come to share in God's holy character. Trusting what God has pledged reshapes our daily conduct to look more like Him.

differ.view: Emphasizes that sharing the divine nature means the restored image of God in holiness and righteousness, rather than becoming divine in essence.
Teaches that believers partake of God's holy character and spiritual life, but humans can never share God's essential divine being.

other.label: Orthodox
other.view: Salvation centers on deification (theosis), where believers are united with God and share in His divine life and energies while remaining distinct created beings.

notes.meaning: Because God has given such great gifts, believers are called to make every effort to grow in their daily walk. Peter describes Christian growth like building blocks, starting with faith and adding moral excellence, spiritual knowledge, self-control, patient endurance, reverence toward God, brotherly affection, and finally genuine love for all people. Love stands as the crown of all these godly traits.

When these godly qualities are present and multiplying, they keep a believer from being idle or useless. Actively practicing these virtues ensures that our knowledge of Jesus Christ produces real spiritual fruit in everyday life.

A person who lacks these virtues suffers from spiritual blindness and can see only earthly things close at hand. Such a person has forgotten the cleansing and forgiveness that Christ provided for their past sins.
Peter urges his readers to be earnest in confirming that God has called and chosen them. Actively cultivating these godly traits protects believers from stumbling in their walk with the Lord.

differ.view: Good works and spiritual growth confirm a believer's personal assurance of God's unchanging election, rather than making God's eternal choice more secure in itself.
Believers must actively persevere in holy living so they do not fall away and lose the calling and election God graciously provided.

notes.meaning: Those who faithfully practice these virtues will receive a rich and joyful welcome into the everlasting kingdom of Jesus Christ. Just as believers generously supply their faith with virtue, God will generously supply their entrance into eternal glory.

Peter explains that he will keep reminding his readers of these essential truths, even though they already know them and stand firm in their faith. Regular reminders help keep believers from becoming careless or forgetful about their spiritual duties.

Peter compares his earthly body to a temporary tent that will soon be set aside in death. The Lord Jesus had previously revealed that Peter would die a martyr's death, so the aging apostle feels an urgent responsibility to stir up his readers while he still has time.

Peter commits to making every effort to preserve his teaching in writing for the church. By leaving this written record, he ensures that believers can easily remember and follow the truth long after he is gone.

The apostles did not rely on clever, man-made myths when they taught about the power and promised return of Jesus. Peter insists that their message was based on hard facts, because they saw Christ's royal majesty with their own eyes.

Peter points to the mountain of transfiguration, where Jesus shone with heavenly glory before his eyes. On that holy mountain, Peter, James, and John heard the voice of God the Father declaring that Jesus is His beloved Son in whom He is well pleased.

In addition to what the apostles saw and heard, believers possess the prophetic words of the Old Testament Scriptures, which have been proven fully reliable. Christians should pay close attention to this written word like a lamp shining in a dark room until Christ returns and His light fills their hearts completely.

No prophecy recorded in Scripture originated from a prophet's own personal thoughts, invention, or human willpower. Instead, holy men spoke directly from God as the Holy Spirit guided and carried them along. Because God is the true author of Scripture, His prophetic word is entirely trustworthy.
